summary: Announces an experimental service that let network users send text to the NIC's Network Journal without logging in to its NLS editing system. Users could submit files from their own computers using mail programs, FTP or Telnet, and the NIC would turn them into journal entries.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 543 describes an experimental way to submit text to the NIC Journal from a network host. Users could also receive Journal messages or citations through network mail, in addition to online or paper delivery.

subtitle: An experimental service for submitting and receiving NIC Journal material by network mail.

tldr.problem: Network users needed a way to submit text to the NIC Journal without entering the NLS system at SRI-ARC.
tldr.mechanism: Users send mail with author and recipient NIC identifiers separated by a slash. SRI-ARC converts accepted mail into an NLS file, catalogs it and notifies the recipients.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a first experimental submission and delivery system, with online, hardcopy and network delivery options.

facts.label: Ways to submit
facts.value: FTP, TELNET, or local mail subsystem

today: The unit records RFC 543's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It documents the first experimental implementation of the Network Journal submission and delivery system.

sections.title: Submitting Text to the Journal
sections.content:
The first implementation of Network Journal Submission and Delivery was experimentally available. It lets network users send text files to the NIC Journal without entering NLS. A user may prepare text on a host system and submit it through a local mail subsystem, FTP or TELNET.

The mail user-name field includes the author's NIC Identifiers before a slash and the recipients' Identifiers after it. The NIC checks the Identifiers. If the slash is absent, the mail is handled as ordinary network mail; if the Identifiers are accepted, the Journal system processes the submission.
sections.plainLanguage: A user can prepare a document on a network computer and send it to the NIC Journal by mail. The slash separates the author's identifier from the recipients' identifiers.

sections.title: How the NIC Processes a Submission
sections.content:
At SRI-ARC, accepted mail is converted into an NLS file, assigned a unique catalog number and stored permanently under that number. The NIC then sends a notice to the listed recipients. A sender may optionally specify a conversion algorithm for turning the sequential message into NLS form.

The first author Ident is treated as the clerk. Invalid Identifiers cause rejection and an error message, after which the user must start again. The RFC also explains that short “Submit Message” items are delivered in full, while longer “Submit File” items are represented by a citation pointing to the Journal document.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC checks the names, converts accepted mail into an NLS document and gives it a catalog number. Recipients get either the complete short message or a citation to a longer document.

sections.title: Journal Delivery Choices
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways to receive Journal material: an online entry in a user's initial file at SRI-ARC, hardcopy sent through the postal service, or network mail delivered to a host and mailbox selected by the user. A user may select one or combine modes.

For longer items delivered over the network, a citation includes the SRI-ARC host and a pathname. The user or a process acting for the user can retrieve the document from the FTP server, which converts the NLS file to sequential form. The NIC keeps delivery host and mailbox settings in the Ident file.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can choose online, paper or network delivery. A network citation can point to a file that the user retrieves from SRI-ARC.
